finding_key: packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts::`get /start` is single-use and method-agnostic, so any duplicate/speculative request silently breaks the login for 30s

verdict.reasoning: The mechanics the claim describes are exactly what the supplied `startCallbackServer` does: the `/start` branch matches on `url.pathname` only (no `req.method` check), sets `startConsumed = true` on the first request that reaches it, and answers every later request `410 START_CONSUMED_MESSAGE`; the 30s timeout only special-cases `sawUnboundCallback`, so a burnt `/start` with no callback ends in the generic "Login timed out" with no mention of the one-time link. That is a genuinely new failure mode — the pre-change code passed the authorize URL straight to `open()`, so a duplicate/HEAD/prefetch fetch could not consume anything — and it is reachable non-adversarially (a HEAD from a scanner, a browser that prefetches an omnibox-pasted URL, a `BROWSER`/launcher that fetches rather than displays, or a reload/back after a hiccup). What I cannot verify is how often those duplicates actually occur, which is the whole of the impact question; the browser at least shows START_CONSUMED_MESSAGE telling the user to re-run, and single-use is a deliberate design choice documented in cli.md, so the cost is a wasted login plus a 30s wait rather than data loss.

Impact is limited to test coverage of a user-facing error message, hence minor; the repository was not browsable here, but login-callback.test.ts is the only test importing `startCallbackServer` per the directory listing.

finding_key: packages/cli/test/login-callback.test.ts::test named "does not crash when a callback arrives before anyone awaits it" never exercises a rejection, so it cannot fail if the `callbackpromise.catch(() => {})` guard is removed

verdict.reasoning: In login-callback.test.ts the test 'does not crash when a callback arrives before anyone awaits it' hits /callback?code=unbound with no state and allowUnbound unset; in login.ts that branch (the `received === null && !options.allowUnbound` block) writes 400 and returns without calling callbackReject, and the test then asserts the promise is still pending after 50ms. The only callbackReject call site is the 30_000ms timeout handler, and the test file uses no fake timers and no 30s wait, so no test in the file ever rejects callbackPromise — the pre-attached `callbackPromise.catch(() => {})` is never exercised and could be deleted with all tests still green. The helper `settledWithin` also attaches its own rejection handler (`promise.then(v=>v, err=>err)`), which would mask an unhandled rejection even if one occurred, reinforcing the point. Impact is limited to test adequacy/misleading comment, not product behaviour.

finding_key: packages/cli/src/client/http-client.ts::`api-keys` commands bypass `send()`, so the session_expired/refresh invariant this delta asserts does not hold for them

verdict.reasoning: Verified in the supplied `packages/cli/src/client/http-client.ts`: `listApiKeys`, `createApiKey` and `revokeApiKey` each call bare `fetch(url, { headers: this.jsonHeaders() })` and return `{ok, status, data}` directly — they never go through `send()`, so no `refreshSession()` retry and no `sessionExpiredBody()` (`{code: 'SESSION_EXPIRED'}`) is ever synthesized for them, unlike `request()`, `uploadFileDocument()` and `downloadFileDocument()`. Consequently the invariant the diff asserts (formatter.ts `forwardUpstreamError` doc comment: "Every command that talks to the backend routes its `!res.ok` branch through here… the client's own 401 `SESSION_EXPIRED` most of all") does not hold for the three `api-keys` subcommands the diff newly routes through the helper: their 401 body is whatever the server sent, which `isErrorEnvelope` will normally reject, yielding `HTTP_ERROR` rather than `SESSION_EXPIRED`, and no refresh is attempted. The new tests stub `fetch` with a fixed status and so never exercise the 401/refresh path, confirming they cannot catch this. Impact is limited (three low-frequency commands, and the missing refresh predates this PR), so I rate it minor rather than a correctness break in the new helper itself.

Impact is limited to one redundant/vacuous assertion in a test that already asserts the real behaviour elsewhere.
